 B.Sudheendra Kumar, J.
The accused Nos.1 and 2 in C.C. No.170 of 2003 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-II,

Aluva filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 read with Rule 44 of the PFA Rules.

2. Heard.
3.

The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 8.1.2002 at about 1 p.m., PW1 the Food Inspector, Aluva Municipality, purchased one Kg. of peas dhal from the shop of the second accused.
First accused was the salesman of the said shop.
After sampling as per rules, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.

The Public Analyst filed Ext. P14 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for peas dhall under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 and therefore, the same was adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 and PW2 were examined and Exts. P1 to P25 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 was examined on the side of the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P14 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P14 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the Afsal vs The Food Inspector on 7 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/78412656/
2 accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

In the result, this Revision Petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act read with Rule 44 of the PFA Rules and the revision petitioners are acquitted for the said offence.
The bail bond of the revision petitioners stands cancelled and they are set at liberty.

Sd/-
 B.SUDHEENDRA KUMAR,
 JUDGE dl/..11.1..2016 // True Copy //
